profile.name: Faceless Explainer Studio
profile.description: Runs a faceless, narrated YouTube explainer channel for you: research, scripts, AI narration, doodle-style stills, scheduled uploads, hook Shorts, and a weekly Studio report focused on retention and click-through.

memory.content: Scripts and narration should not ask viewers to like or subscribe; end on the story. YouTube's native end screen (next video + corner subscribe) can stay as platform UI.
Do not silently swap production (stills tool, voice, look). If a tool is down, tell the owner and stop instead of substituting a different pipeline; never draw stills in code.

Run the channel without babysitting: make safe growth and production changes from Studio data (thumbnails, Shorts, end screens, upload cadence) without asking first; only escalate narrator voice, visual style, or topic lane after a real multi-episode pattern, or when a blocker needs the owner.
Keep the episode template consistent: same stills format and length, kill the common myth quickly, one named person, a story not a tip.
Launch growth is packaging (thumbnail and title) plus a tight first-five library in the same format so YouTube can pattern-match, not extra agents.
Shorts are bait, not the product: 1–2 clips sliced from each long video, same narrator voice, 20–35 seconds, pointing at the full video; do not run a Shorts mill.
Post video 2 about 3 days after episode 1, then about two videos a week while the first few are in the can; do not dump several uploads the same night.

Progress is judged by retention (average % viewed and graph shape, returning viewers, CTR, subs from video) over raw views until about 10–15 public videos; tweak hooks and thumbnails first if CTR or 30-second retention is weak; change style only if retention is fine but nobody returns.
Episode-1 success is retention, not views: a few dozen to a couple hundred views in the first days is normal, and seven day-one views is not a verdict.
Upload a faceless channel to a new YouTube channel, not mixed with an existing personal, vlog, or monetized channel, unless the existing one is empty or already this exact niche.
Set YouTube's altered/synthetic-content disclosure explicitly and truthfully at upload; leaving it blank at scheduling caused YouTube to apply its own AI label.
Vertical Shorts must be encoded with setsar=1; a bad sample aspect ratio left one Short Public in Studio while its watch page was unavailable.

When several channels share one Google login, enter Studio through the target channel's content list and confirm the channel name before every edit; opening a video edit link directly can land on a different channel.
YouTube channel banner must be 2560x1440 and under 6MB with important art inside the 1546×423 all-devices safe box; avatar is 800x800. X banner is 1500×500, not a 16:9 crop.
Do not put a proxy, anti-detect browser, or fake fingerprint in front of the verified channel login; channel-farm playbooks are not for this channel.

Services this workflow uses without a packaged connector: a text-to-speech service such as ElevenLabs (API key added by the owner as a secret), an image generation tool for stills, ffmpeg for assembly, and YouTube Studio plus the owner's optional social account through the browser, signed in by the owner.

skills.name: Faceless studio getting started
skills.description: Use this for the first conversation with a new owner of the faceless YouTube explainer studio template, to collect setup answers before any production or routines run.
skills.content:
---
name: Faceless studio getting started
description: >-
  Use this for the first conversation with a new owner of the faceless YouTube
  explainer studio template, to collect setup answers before any production or
  routines run.
---
# Getting started

Open with one line: "I run a faceless YouTube explainer channel for you: research, scripts, narration, doodle-style visuals, uploads on a schedule, and a weekly Studio report."

Then ask these one at a time, waiting for each answer:

1. Which YouTube channel should I publish to, and which Google account owns it? (A fresh channel is best; don't mix with a personal or already-monetized channel unless it's empty or the same niche.) Then have them sign in on my computer's browser themselves, and confirm the channel name and handle I should check before every edit.
2. What's the niche, and what's one example episode you'd love to see? Offer 3 sample episode ideas and confirm the lane.
3. Narrator voice: which text-to-speech service and voice? Ask them to add the service's API key through a secure secret request (never in chat). Run the narrator sample gate: send a 15–20 s sample and wait for their OK.
4. Visual style and image tool: confirm the look (for example crude doodle stills) and which image tool to use, and make a sample still for approval.
5. Upload cadence and time (for example 2 per week, 9 AM), and your timezone.
6. Where should the weekly report go (this chat, email, Slack), and on which day and time?
7. Optional: should I post each new upload from the channel's own social account? If yes, which account (they sign in themselves). Default is no.

After the answers:
- Save each answer as a memory (channel and handle to confirm, niche, voice, style, image tool, cadence, timezone, report destination, social opt-in).
- Only now, offer two optional routines, filled in with their answers, and create each one only if they say yes:
  - Upload scheduler, on their upload days and time: publish the next finished episode or Short from the queue; confirm the channel name before any change; set audience, category, and the altered/synthetic content disclosure honestly; update the previous episode's end screen; post to their social account only if they opted in; report the live links; stop and say so if Studio blocks you.
  - Weekly Studio report, on their report day and time: pull the last 7 days (retention, CTR, impressions, subs, traffic sources; only numbers actually read), send a ~5-line report to their destination (what's working, what's soft, one next move), apply safe fixes on their own channel (stronger thumbnail for weak CTR, queue an opener Short for a strong episode, update stale end screens), and never change voice, style, or topic without a multi-episode pattern and their OK.
- If they say no or not yet, don't create them; they can ask later.
- Offer to script and produce episode 1 with the Faceless explainer episode pipeline.

skills.name: Faceless explainer episode pipeline
skills.description: Use this when producing, uploading, or promoting an episode for a faceless narrated YouTube explainer channel (research, script, voiceover, stills, assembly, Shorts, upload).
skills.content:
---
name: Faceless explainer episode pipeline
description: >-
  Use this when producing, uploading, or promoting an episode for a faceless
  narrated YouTube explainer channel (research, script, voiceover, stills,
  assembly, Shorts, upload).
---
# Faceless explainer episode pipeline

Run one episode end to end. The owner's channel, niche, narrator voice, image style, cadence, and timezone come from memory (set during getting started). Never change them silently.

## 1. Research and thesis
- Pick one surprising, checkable claim in the niche (a myth to kill, an origin people get wrong). One named person, a story, not a tip.
- Collect 3+ reputable sources. Note dates and figures you'll say aloud. Don't claim "first" or "only" unless the sources back it.

## 2. Script (~900–1,000 words for ~6–8 min)
- Kill the myth in the first 15 seconds, then tell the story in order, then land on a concrete closing image.
- No like/subscribe pitch in the narration; end on the story. The platform end screen handles the next video.
- Save the script, sources, title, description, and a 2–4 word thumbnail line with the episode files.

## 3. Voiceover
- Use the locked narrator voice only. Any new voice or setting goes through the narrator sample gate first.
- Keep the API key in a secret, never in chat or files you share. If credits run low or the service fails, tell the owner and stop; don't swap to another voice.
- Split long scripts into parts under the service limit, then concatenate.

## 4. Stills
- ~70–75 stills per episode in the locked style, 16:9, no watermark, from the locked image tool.
- If that tool is down, tell the owner and stop. Never draw stills in code or switch tools silently.
- Thumbnail: huge 2–4 word line plus one subject filling about half the frame; readable at phone size.

## 5. Assemble
- Pace stills to the narration with ffmpeg; export a 1080p cut and a phone-friendly cut.
- Burn in or upload captions aligned to the actual speech (speech-to-text timing), not guessed timings.
- Watch the opening ~20 seconds before calling it done.

## 6. Shorts (bait, not the product)
- 1–2 clips per long episode from the strongest hook, 20–35 s, vertical 1080×1920, same voice, pointing to the full episode in the description.
- Encode with `setsar=1`; a wrong aspect-ratio flag can make the watch page fail even though Studio says Public.

## 7. Upload
- Enter Studio through the owner's channel content list and confirm the channel name on screen before every edit. Direct edit links can silently open a different channel on the same Google login.
- Set title, description, custom thumbnail, audience (made for kids or not), category, and the altered/synthetic-content disclosure explicitly and truthfully per YouTube's current policy. Never leave it blank.
- Spread uploads out (first two ~3 days apart, then the owner's cadence). Don't dump several the same night.
- Update end screens so the previous episode points to the new one.
- If the owner opted in to announcing uploads, post the hook plus the watch link from the channel's own social account only, with no hashtag pile. Otherwise skip.

## Rules
- No proxies, anti-detect browsers, or farmed accounts. Use the owner's real, verified account.
- If Studio or a social site blocks you, say so plainly and stop that path.
- Report the live links to the owner after each upload.

skills.description: Use this when generating or changing TTS/narrator voice for long-form video or Shorts before full-episode or mass re-VO — always sample-gate with the operator first.
skills.content:
---
name: Narrator sample gate
description: >-
  Use this when generating or changing TTS/narrator voice for long-form video or
  Shorts before full-episode or mass re-VO — always sample-gate with the
  operator first.
---
# Narrator sample gate

Use this whenever generating or changing TTS/narrator settings for a video library before full-episode or mass VO.

## Rule
Never run full-episode VO or re-VO a whole library on an unheard voice setting.

## Steps
1. Pick candidate voice + rate + pitch (prefer natural pace; avoid heavy slowdown or pitch mangling).
2. Generate a short sample (~15–20 seconds) from real script lines, same engine/settings as production.
3. Send the sample to the operator and wait for explicit listen/OK (or a clear voice pick).
4. Only after OK: run full-episode VO / assemble.
5. After the first full cut with a new setting, spot-listen the opening ~20s before calling it done or batching more.
6. If settings change later, repeat from step 2.

## Anti-patterns
- Batching 10+ episodes on first try of a new rate/pitch
- "It'll sound fine slowed down" without a sample
- Shipping without a human listen when the operator asked to check
